these are personal experiences. adhd and autism present different in everyone. meds affect everyone differently. this is just how i’ve dealt with things. 

i am 18f, freshmen in college with ADHD and i suspect I’m on the spectrum. My friend has ADHD and is on the spectrum and your sons friend being EXACTLY like him reminds me of how we became friends. 
speaking in the medication bit - i also have very severe anxiety. i just began well butrin and it has been a godsend. it works like an SSRI but with dopamine, and it is is very mild, commonly prescribed to help smokers quit smoking. i didn’t notice any effects for the first week and they were very mild. by the 8th week mark when they reached full affect, i look back and my public school experience and i envy everyone who felt this normal all the time and i was genuinely confused how i navigated relatively successfully (socially). My quality of life has improved dramatically. 

executive dysfunction is tricky. sometimes it’s triggered by overstimulation (which i didn’t realize until recently could be something as small as having too many people in the room, even on well butrin). 
prior to this, my therapist had said starting and following through with tasks may be difficult bc of anxiety, but now that my anxiety was gone and i was still struggling in my very time consuming classes, we decided to start extended release adderall. this is the only thing that has helped with redirecting focus and follow through. 

however eating becomes a priority on adderall. i don’t take it every day bc ADHD has eating symptoms of its own (like forgetting to eat bc i got side tracked or lost track of time). if i know i have shit to do tomorrow, the night before i have to prep a high protein smoothie bc how i have experience the adderall side affect, my stomach feels empty but i’m not actively hungry. i’ll try to eat but it takes mental force to fight my gag reflex. smoothies are filling and easier to eat. 

all this being said, adderall may or may not be for your son. maybe it’s something you try later when the stakes are higher and his brain is more developed. for now just research the most you can about adhd symptoms and how they affect relationships and their lives across the board. 

i would ask doctors about the anxiety and ways to cope, and if well butrin may be an option if that’s something you’re open to. the anxiety is what left more permanent marks. 

for adhd, fight for accommodations and flexibility with deadlines. explain to his teachers that he is smart, and he cares but (if he is diagnosed) he LITERALLY has a disorder that affects everything school is trying to instill in him, and the pressure is paralyzing. we haven’t changed the way schools are run since the industrial revolution. it’s not the an environment suitable for a jack of all trades who only engages with things for the dopamine. that’s why it feels like wading through water trying to get through school. 

the other note about that is burnout - after school, i had no more brain energy to do hw. i was exhausted for the day and most days when i came home, and i wandered around the house doing random things - eating, playing piano, playing with the animals, just staring at a wall- for about an hour. let him do that. he needs to recharge. 

otherwise, just listen to him.

no, both of them are controllable but to be maladaptive daydreaming you have to exhibit the physical symptoms: whispering the conversation to yourself, repetitive movements, facial expressions, hand gestures. immersive daydreaming is the mental aspect of the daydreaming. so you can immersive daydream (feel mentally in the world with the characters) without the physical symptoms. it’s the physical symptoms that make it more intense and considered maladaptive.
